data.targetWord: A disciple or learner; a follower of the teachings of the Ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib

examples.en-GB: There are approximately 800,000 Sikhs in Britain.

data.targetWord: The foundational statement of Sikh belief meaning 'There is one God', which opens the Guru Granth Sahib

examples.en-GB: Ik Onkar is represented by a special symbol at the start of the Sikh scripture.

data.targetWord: The Sikh name for God, meaning 'Wonderful Lord', expressing wonder, awe, and devotion

examples.en-GB: Sikhs meditate on the name Waheguru as an act of Naam Japna.

data.targetWord: The first pillar of Sikhism — meditating on and reciting God's name, staying conscious of God in daily life

examples.en-GB: A Sikh may practise Naam Japna by reciting Waheguru during daily tasks.

data.targetWord: The second pillar of Sikhism — earning a living through honest, hard work without deception or exploitation

examples.en-GB: Kirat Karni means refusing to take shortcuts or deceive others in business.

data.targetWord: The third pillar of Sikhism — sharing one's wealth, time, and resources with those in need

examples.en-GB: Serving in the langar is an expression of Vand Chakna.

data.targetWord: The first Sikh Guru and founder of Sikhism (1469–1539), who received a divine call to spread the message of one God and human equality

examples.en-GB: Guru Nanak travelled widely teaching that there is one God and all humans are equal.

data.targetWord: The eternal, living Guru and sacred scripture of the Sikhs, declared the permanent Guru by Guru Gobind Singh in 1708

examples.en-GB: The Guru Granth Sahib is treated with the reverence due to a living person of the highest spiritual authority.

data.targetWord: The community of initiated Sikhs founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, committed to upholding Sikh values and protecting the oppressed

examples.en-GB: Khalsa Sikhs take the name Singh (lion) or Kaur (princess) and wear the Five Ks.

data.targetWord: The Sikh place of worship and community centre, meaning 'Gateway of the Guru', containing a prayer hall and langar

examples.en-GB: Every gurdwara has a Nishan Sahib flag flying outside to identify it.

data.targetWord: Selfless service to others, performed as an act of worship; one of the most important Sikh ethical principles

examples.en-GB: Volunteers who cook and serve food in the langar are performing sewa.

data.targetWord: The free communal kitchen in every gurdwara, serving vegetarian food to all people regardless of faith, caste, or wealth

examples.en-GB: The langar is open to everyone — a living expression of equality and service.

data.targetWord: The holy community of worshippers who gather together in the gurdwara; the congregation

examples.en-GB: Sangat reinforces equality — all sit together regardless of social status.

data.targetWord: Sitting in a row together when eating in the langar, so that everyone is at the same level and no one is elevated above others

examples.en-GB: Pangat makes equality visible — even important guests sit on the floor like everyone else.

data.targetWord: Devotional singing of shabads (hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib) performed by musicians as an act of worship

examples.en-GB: Kirtan is performed in the gurdwara using traditional instruments such as the harmonium and tabla.

data.targetWord: The person who reads the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara; does not need to be specially ordained

examples.en-GB: Women can serve as granthis — reading the Guru Granth Sahib — reflecting Sikh equality.

data.targetWord: Five articles of faith worn by initiated Khalsa Sikhs, each beginning with the Punjabi letter K: Kesh, Kanga, Kara, Kachera, Kirpan

examples.en-GB: Each of the Five Ks carries a specific spiritual meaning related to commitment, purity, and justice.

data.targetWord: Uncut hair, one of the Five Ks, symbolising acceptance of God's will and respect for the body as God created it

examples.en-GB: Many Khalsa Sikh men cover their Kesh with a turban as a mark of identity.

data.targetWord: A steel bracelet, one of the Five Ks, worn as a reminder of God's infinity and the Sikh commitment to righteous action

examples.en-GB: The Kara is circular with no beginning or end, representing the eternal nature of Waheguru.

data.targetWord: A small ceremonial sword, one of the Five Ks, symbolising the commitment to justice and the defence of the oppressed

examples.en-GB: The Kirpan is a religious symbol of courage and justice, not a weapon for violence.

data.targetWord: The most important Sikh festival, celebrated in April, marking the harvest and the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699

examples.en-GB: Vaisakhi is celebrated with nagar kirtan processions, prayers, and langar.

data.targetWord: An anniversary day commemorating the birth or martyrdom of one of the ten Sikh Gurus, celebrated with continuous scripture reading and langar

examples.en-GB: Guru Nanak Gurpurb celebrates the birthday of the first Guru with nagar kirtan.

data.targetWord: The Sikh flag flown outside every gurdwara, displaying the Khanda symbol on an orange background

examples.en-GB: The Nishan Sahib tells the community where the gurdwara is located.

data.targetWord: A formal Sikh prayer recited standing with hands together at the end of every religious gathering, ceremony, or significant moment

examples.en-GB: Ardas is said at the end of every service in the gurdwara.

data.targetWord: The opening passage of the Guru Granth Sahib and the fundamental statement of Sikh theology, declaring the oneness and nature of God

examples.en-GB: The Mool Mantar begins 'There is one God. Truth is His name. He is the Creator.'

data.title: Place these events in the history of Sikhism in the correct order
items: Guru Nanak receives a divine call and begins teaching Ik Onkar
Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiles the Adi Granth and builds the Harmandir Sahib
Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa at Vaisakhi
Guru Gobind Singh declares the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru

data.title: Put these steps in the correct order for a visit to a gurdwara
items: Remove shoes and cover your head at the entrance
Enter the darbar sahib and bow before the Guru Granth Sahib
Sit on the floor with the sangat to listen to kirtan
Go to the langar hall and share a meal with the community

data.title: Arrange the steps in the langar process in the correct order
items: Volunteers prepare and cook the vegetarian food
Everyone sits on the floor together in rows (pangat)
Food is served equally to all present
Volunteers wash up — continuing their sewa
